context: process-piping & pump-led · membrane commissioning drives the ramp to spec

brief.intro: A desalination plant makes potable or process water from seawater or brackish water, most commonly by reverse osmosis (RO) — high-pressure pumps forcing water through membranes — or, less commonly, thermal distillation. The programme is dominated by extensive process piping (intake, pretreatment, high-pressure, product and brine/outfall lines) and pumping equipment, with marine intake/outfall works and basin structures as the defining civil interface. The critical path runs through pretreatment mechanical completion, into high-pressure pump and RO train installation, into membrane loading — often one of the last, most schedule-sensitive steps — into chemical dosing and post-treatment, and finally into product-water quality verification against contracted spec. The plant is only proven once real water has flowed through it end to end at sustained output.

scope.name: Intake & pretreatment
scope.desc: Seawater or brackish intake works, screening, coagulation/flocculation, and media or membrane pretreatment filters.

scope.name: High-pressure pumping
scope.desc: HP feed pumps and energy recovery devices that drive water through the RO membranes.

scope.name: RO train / membrane skids
scope.desc: Pressure vessels, membrane elements and racks — the core desalination process.

scope.name: Chemical dosing
scope.desc: Antiscalant, coagulant, chlorination/dechlorination and clean-in-place chemical systems.

scope.name: Post-treatment & remineralization
scope.desc: Stabilizing product water to potable or process spec — pH and hardness.

scope.name: Product water storage & distribution
scope.desc: Clearwell/product tanks and pumping to the distribution network.

scope.name: Brine / concentrate outfall
scope.desc: Managing and discharging the concentrated reject stream, often via a marine outfall.

scope.name: Electrical & power supply
scope.desc: MV/LV distribution sized for the large HP pump loads, often the plant's biggest single load.

scope.name: Instrumentation & control (SCADA)
scope.desc: Process control, membrane performance monitoring and alarms.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: Pretreatment proving, HP system pressure test, membrane loading and wet commissioning, product-water quality verification.

must_get_right: Sequence pretreatment ahead of HP/RO — feeding unfiltered water into membranes, even briefly, can cause irreversible fouling.
Protect membrane loading as a distinct, late, labour-intensive milestone — it happens after all HP piping is flushed and pressure-tested, not in parallel with pipework.
Treat product-water quality verification, not mechanical completion, as the real finish line — the plant isn't done until sustained output meets the contracted spec, which needs a real trial run.
Start marine intake/outfall civil works early — they are long-duration and sit on the critical path to first water in.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Marine civil works follow tide and weather windows for intake and outfall construction; mechanical/piping erection runs 6-day weeks with two shifts at peak on HP piping and RO racking; commissioning — from pressure test through membrane loading — runs a continuous 7-day calendar to protect the wet-commissioning sequence.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs intake/outfall marine civil → pretreatment mechanical completion → HP piping hydrotest & flush → membrane element loading → wet commissioning (first permeate) → chemical dosing & post-treatment proving → product-water quality verification to contracted spec. Membrane loading is scheduled only after the HP system is proven clean and pressure-tested, since contamination at that stage damages membranes.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Feed-water quality data and design basis are fixed before RO-train sizing; a single mobilisation; marine works comply with environmental/permit windows already secured; and no late change to product-water recovery rate or capacity that would resize pumps or membranes.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Intake and outfall works are constrained by marine access, tide windows and environmental permit conditions. Membrane loading needs a clean, dust-free, access-controlled environment and specialist technicians — a scarce resource scheduled as a discrete, non-compressible activity. HP piping fabrication may require offsite spooling and controlled site welding/hydrotest windows.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: marine works slippage from weather/tide windows, membrane contamination or damage during loading, and product-water quality trial results falling short of spec (requiring a dosing or operational re-tune). Contingency is held before membrane loading and before the final product-water quality trial rather than spread across piping activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
